title.text: Americans and Soviets in the Space Age

textContent.text: On July 20, 1969, televisions across the world glowed with the same shadowy scene as millions watched the hazy image of a man in a spacesuit stepping off a ladder and onto the surface of the moon. The American astronaut then announced to the world, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Indeed, that moment demonstrated an accomplishment that no human being had ever achieved before. That astronaut's first moon step also marked a great step in a race that had started years earlier.

It all began in Moscow, in 1903, when an inventor named Konstantin Tsiolkovsky came up with the idea of creating rockets to launch into space. Tsiolkovsky's ideas went untested until 1926, when an American scientist named Robert Goddard built and launched the first successful rocket. This event would become the first in a series of worldwide demonstrations by countries hoping to show off their superior space technology.

During much of the twentieth century, the United States' chief rival in these demonstrations was the Soviet Union. This country, which officially disbanded in 1991, was formerly made up of Russia and fourteen other republics in eastern Europe and Asia. Although there was no official contest between the two countries, their rivalry became known as "the Space Race." Most of the early victories in the Space Race went to the Soviet Union. In 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 1, the first space satellite. Then, in 1961, they struck another devastating blow when they put the first person into orbit around the Earth, just weeks before the United States sent its own astronaut into orbit.

Weeks after this close loss to the Soviet Union, President John F. Kennedy declared that the United States would be the first nation to put a person on the moon, and it would do so by the end of the 1960s. This was an audacious goal for NASA, the United States' space program, to achieve. With the Soviet Union getting off to an early lead, the United States seemed to be the underdog in the Space Race. The announcement was especially bold since the U.S. had only recently sent an astronaut into space for the first time, and the flight had only lasted for fifteen minutes. However, with the support of the U.S. government and the enthusiasm of the American people, NASA was determined to succeed.

NASA launched many space missions throughout the 1960s. Some of these initial missions failed, but out of each failure came new lessons and opportunities. And eventually, NASA began to achieve some victories in the Space Race. For example, Gemini 8 became the first spacecraft to successfully dock with another craft while in orbit. Missions like this helped advance NASA's knowledge and technology, setting the stage for the remarkable first moon landing in 1969.

While no winner was ever declared in the Space Race, many consider the U.S. moon landing to be one of the greatest achievements in the history of space exploration. However, both the United States and the Soviet Union made great scientific advancements during the competition. Today, most space projects come from cooperation, rather than competition, between countries. While nations continue to take pride in their individual space programs, most are also interested in working together to explore the worlds that exist beyond our own.

textContent.text: Like many powerful leaders of the past, King Kamehameha I of Hawaii is a ruler associated with great myths and legends. According to one story, strange lights appeared in the sky when he was born. Another legend tells of how he overturned a seven-thousand-pound stone to prove his place as the rightful ruler of Hawaii. While we may never know the truth of these stories, Kamehameha's achievements have earned him a place among history's great rulers.

pieces.text: Before Kamehameha's time, various high chiefs, or

(pronounced ah-LEE-ee), ruled different areas of Hawaii's major islands: the "Big Island" of Hawai'i, Kaua'i, Oahu, Moloka'i, Lanai, and Maui. Upon the death of an ali'i, new chiefs were appointed and land was redistributed. These events were often followed by bitter battles for power and control. As a result, periods of peace frequently alternated with periods of war, creating instability among the Hawaiian people.

textContent.text: In 1782, the head ali'i on the island of Hawai'i died. Before his death, though, he made a stunning decision—he split his power between his son, Kiwalao, and his favored nephew, Kamehameha. This caused a conflict between the two young men, which other ali'i tried to take advantage of when it came to determining how land was to be redistributed. A bitter battle ensued over control of the island of Hawai'i. Even though Kiwalao died early in the battle, the remaining ali'i continued to struggle for full control of Hawaii's largest island. Finally, after eight grueling years of fighting, Kamehameha gained total power over the island.

Even though Hawaiians lived in separate territories within the island chain, they shared similar religious and cultural practices. As Kamehameha came to power on the island of Hawai'i, other ali'i fought for power on the other islands. Kamehameha saw that the constant fighting was harming the Hawaiian people. He believed that for there to be lasting peace, the islands should be united under a single ruler. He was determined to be that leader, hoping that a swift, decisive military victory would put an end to the fighting.

The late 1700s saw the arrival of foreigners to the Hawaiian islands. Many traders and explorers stopped in Hawaii during their travels to and from the Americas and Asia. These newcomers introduced new weapons like guns, cannons, and warships, changing the way Hawaiians fought.

Kamehameha took advantage of these new weapons in his quest to unite the islands. He stockpiled the weapons and recruited foreigners to help him with military strategy. With the aid of new equipment, new ideas about warfare, and the support of a religious council, Kamehameha became a powerful military leader. He continued his quest to unite the other islands through force and strategic negotiation, and by 1795, he also controlled the islands of Maui, Oahu, Lanai, and Moloka'i.

With five of the six major islands successfully united, Kamehameha set his sights on the island of Kaua'i. To prepare for this fight, he built modern ships and armed his warriors with muskets. The anticipated battle never happened, however, because Kamehameha reached an agreement with Kaua'i's leader. It was decided that the current ali'i would continue to lead Kaua'i, but Kamehameha would reign over him. By 1810, Kamehameha had successfully unified the Hawaiian islands.

At long last, the people of Hawaii were at peace and Kamehameha could now focus on economic and political development. He promoted Hawaii as a new global trading port, which significantly strengthened the Hawaiian economy. He honored ancient cultural systems while creating a new government structure for Hawaii.
King Kamehameha's reign came to an end when he died in 1819, but his legacy of a unified Hawaii remains to this day.

textContent.text: At the end of a long winter, most people look forward to the relief of a nice, warm summer. Bizarrely, in the year 1816, that relief never came for much of the northern hemisphere.

This "Year Without a Summer" struck the northeastern United States hard. In the spring, the air warmed and flowers bloomed like normal. But in early June, a massive snowstorm blew into New England, dropping more than a foot of snow in some areas. In fact, some locations reported snowdrifts twenty inches deep. The weather began to warm again, but soon more cold weather arrived. On the Fourth of July, temperatures were so chilly that people playing horseshoes outside were bundled up in winter coats.

The farmers of Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont were not accustomed to harsh summer snowstorms. The June storm destroyed many of their crops, and in August, severe frost killed most of the remaining plants. The cold summer weather impacted farm animals in the region as well. Some animals were not able to survive the freezing temperatures, while others suffered from starvation due to the crop shortages.

Like the farm animals, the people in New England struggled to find food. The harsh weather left the roads in such poor shape that it was almost impossible to import food from warmer regions. This predicament forced many people to become creative with their eating habits. Some turned to harvesting wild plants, while others ate pigeons and raccoons for sustenance. Many New Englanders were so distressed that they moved west. Tens of thousands of people ended up migrating westward to the Ohio and Indiana territories, leaving entire towns nearly deserted.

pieces.text: This bizarre weather was not limited to the United States. Much of Europe and parts of Asia also experienced dark, cold, and stormy weather in 1816. Some people worried that the sun was failing and that the world was coming to an end. The gloomy skies inspired poems and stories still popular today. During this time, a young author named Mary Shelley was vacationing with a group of writer friends in Switzerland. For entertainment, the guests started a writing contest. Inspired by the strange and stormy weather, Shelley began work on her now-famous horror story

. The English poet Lord Byron also composed a famous piece of writing that year. Byron's poem "Darkness" begins with the lines, "I had a dream, which was not all a dream. The bright sun was extinguish'd," which captured people's fears about the dimming of the sun.

textContent.text: Despite what many thought, the dim, cold summer was not the end of the world. So, what was actually happening in 1816? At the time, some scientists blamed sunspots for the darkened skies. However, historians and meteorologists now believe that the weather disruptions actually resulted from a massive volcanic eruption. In April 1815, Indonesia's 13,000-foot Mt. Tambora exploded in the greatest volcanic eruption in recorded history. The blast created a crater more than three miles wide and caused an enormous cloud of ash and dust to explode into the air. Long after the eruption, the ash and dust remained in the atmosphere, reflecting the sun's light and heat back into space. This caused the temperature on Earth to lower as the ash and dust particles spread across the globe. In 1816, over a year after the blast, enough debris remained to block out much of the sunlight, resulting in a year where summer never came.

title.text: Layers of Discovery at Sutton Hoo

textContent.text: The discovery of an Anglo-Saxon ship at the Sutton Hoo burial site is one of the greatest archeological discoveries in the history of England. The ship found at Sutton Hoo dates back to the seventh century, during a time period in Europe sometimes referred to as the Dark Ages. The discovery of the ship and the items within it forever altered our understanding of the Anglo-Saxon people and the time period in which they lived.

The discovery started with a simple request; in 1939, a landowner who lived in an area known as Sutton Hoo asked an amateur archaeologist, Basil Brown, to excavate and examine a burial mound on her property. A burial mound is a human-made hill that covers the remains of the dead. While they are not unheard of in countries as old as England, this one was extraordinary. In their excavation, Brown and the landowner uncovered a treasure trove of objects.

Carefully removing layers of dirt, Brown and his helpers were shocked to discover an enormous wooden ship measuring over eighty-eight feet long. The center of the ship held a burial chamber that had collapsed over time, but in its remains Brown's team found ornate silverware, textiles, weapons and armor, drinking horns, and gold coins. While some objects were broken or had eroded, others were almost as pristine as they had been when they were buried thirteen centuries earlier. Brown and other archeologists wanted to figure out who was buried at Sutton Hoo and what the world had been like when the mound was built.

Whoever was laid to rest at Sutton Hoo was undeniably important in the Anglo-Saxon world. Some historians speculate that the person buried there was an Anglo-Saxon king. While we may never know for sure, we do know that great effort and resources went into the burial. A large ship was hauled uphill from the river, a burial chamber was built within it, and magnificent riches were placed inside. Finally, a massive hill was raised around the ship. Some of the items in the chamber—like an ornate helmet and a beautifully decorated iron sword—attest to the importance of its occupant. However, the objects in the tomb also tell a much broader story as well.

At the time of the Sutton Hoo discovery, many scholars believed there was little advancement in Anglo-Saxon culture between the fifth and tenth centuries—hence the historical term "Dark Ages." However, the treasures at Sutton Hoo indicated something different. As the archeologists pieced together fragments of objects, they also put together new ideas about the Anglo-Saxons and their world. The Sutton Hoo burial mound held jewels from Sri Lanka, a country off the coast of India. There was silverware from the Byzantine Empire in the Middle East and coins from all across Europe. The helmet and sword found at the site feature artistic designs that are difficult to match—even with today's tools. Together, these items suggest that the Anglo-Saxons were more knowledgeable and had a more complex culture than previously believed. The burial mound at Sutton Hoo contained many rare and expensive objects. But the real treasure was what it taught us about the past.

textContent.text: The discovery of an Anglo-Saxon ship at the Sutton Hoo burial site is one of the greatest archeological discoveries in the history of England. The ship found at Sutton Hoo dates back to the seventh century, during a time period in Europe sometimes referred to as the Dark Ages. The discovery started with a simple request; in 1939, a landowner who lived in an area known as Sutton Hoo asked an amateur archaeologist, Basil Brown, to excavate and examine a burial mound on her property. A burial mound is a human-made hill that covers the remains of the dead. While they are not unheard of in countries as old as England, this one was extraordinary. In their excavation, Brown and the landowner uncovered a treasure trove of objects.

Carefully removing layers of dirt, Brown and his helpers were shocked to discover an enormous wooden ship measuring over eighty-eight feet long. The center of the ship held a burial chamber that had collapsed over time, but in its remains Brown's team found ornate silverware, textiles, weapons and armor, drinking horns, and gold coins. While some objects were broken or had eroded, others were almost as pristine as they had been when they were buried thirteen centuries earlier. Brown and other archeologists wanted to figure out who was buried at Sutton Hoo and what the world had been like when the mound was built.

Some of the items in the chamber—like an ornate helmet and a beautifully decorated iron sword—attest to the importance of its occupant. Together, these items suggest that the Anglo-Saxons were more knowledgeable and had a more complex culture than previously believed. textContent.text: A preserved pigeon with a missing leg sits in a display case in the National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. What is this one-legged bird doing in the museum? It is Cher Ami, a messenger pigeon who captured the attention of the world during World War I.

World War I, fought between 1914 and 1918, involved more than thirty European countries. In 1917, the United States joined the war to help defend France and other allies against Germany. On the European battlefields, it was difficult to communicate across long distances. Telegraphs could not be sent in places where there were no telegraph wires, and signal flags did not work well when it was dark or stormy. Human messengers were an option, but they had trouble getting through areas with active fighting. That is when trained homing pigeons came to the rescue.

Homing pigeons possess the remarkable ability to find their way home, even after traveling great distances. Though scientists still do not entirely understand how pigeons navigate, people have known about pigeons' amazing homing ability for centuries. During World War I, some pigeons flew with small cameras strapped to their chests, bringing back photographs of enemy positions. However, the pigeons' primary job was to carry messages. In battle, an officer would write a note on a small piece of paper, which would then be inserted into a canister attached to a pigeon's leg. When the bird was then released into the air, it flew "home" to military headquarters.

Pigeons were ideally suited for wartime work. They were easy to carry and feed during troop movements. In addition, the birds were fast and reliable, reaching speeds of up to sixty miles per hour. Many wartime homing pigeons sustained injuries during their flights. However, these wounded birds still continued their missions. Cher Ami, whose name means "dear friend" in French, was one of those heroic birds.

In October 1917, a company of five hundred American soldiers commanded by Major Charles Whittlesey was advancing against German troops in France. The Americans, suffering heavy losses and running out of food and water, found themselves surrounded by German forces.

The company had several pigeons, and Whittlesey began sending them to his commanders with reports and pleas for help. Although headquarters ordered reinforcements, the additional troops failed to reach the company. To save the trapped soldiers, the American command ordered their large guns to fire on the Germans. Although at first Whittlesey was relieved, he quickly realized the American bombardment was hitting his own men.

Whittlesey had just one pigeon left—Cher Ami. The major wrote a final message: "We are along the road parallel 276.4. Our artillery is dropping a barrage directly on us. For heaven's sake, stop it." Cher Ami flew off to take this vital information to the battle commanders. As Whittlesey watched Cher Ami's departure, German soldiers also spotted the pigeon and took aim. Shots rang out, and Cher Ami plummeted. As the soldiers watched in alarm, the bird recovered, gained altitude, and kept flying.

Cher Ami arrived at headquarters twenty-five minutes later, with an injured eye and a wounded leg. But the message was still safely in its canister. Cher Ami had succeeded in delivering Whittlesey's plea to stop shooting. When American artillery fire stopped, Whittlesey and his soldiers cheered. Cher Ami had saved them, they said.

Once safe, American medics cared tenderly for Cher Ami's wounds, and when the bird's injured leg had to be removed, they carved a small wooden leg to replace it. The story of that brave flight under fire earned Cher Ami a place in the National Museum of American History and made the small bird one of the most well-known heroes of the war.

pieces.text: In the year 1368, a new era began in China. After taking back the country from the Mongols, the emperor, Taizu, envisioned a new time for China that would expand the country's presence in the world. Taizu decided to name the new era

, meaning "great brightness." Taizu was the first in the line of emperors known as the Ming dynasty, which ruled China for nearly three hundred years. The Ming dynasty became known for its bold emperors, its expanded global trade network, and its world-renowned works of art and architecture. This magnificent dynasty made long lasting impacts throughout China and beyond.

textContent.text: The emperors of the Ming dynasty made their power and influence clear to their subjects and those beyond their rule. At the beginning of the dynasty, emperors ruled from the city of Nanjing. Then, the emperor Zhu Di made a bold decision to move the seat of power to Beijing. There, he started construction on a grand palace for the new capital city. The palace and nearly one hundred accompanying buildings were surrounded by tall, dark-red walls and giant gates that kept out all but the royal family and high-ranking elites. This new center of politics and culture became known as the Forbidden City. This magnificent complex was a central part of China's political and social landscape until the early 1900s.

One of the most important Ming leaders was Emperor Yongle. Most of the dynasty's influence outside of China can be traced back to him. Emperor Yongle helped open up trade between China and other countries by sending maritime trade ships throughout Asia and eastern Africa. These sea expeditions led to an ongoing exchange of goods and ideas that influenced cultures around the world.

One of the goods exported during the Ming dynasty even became a kind of national symbol of China. Chinese artists used local clay and refinement techniques to create bowls, plates, and vases made of smooth porcelain. This pottery was often bright white and blue, with elaborate images of dragons and lotus flowers. This form of Chinese art was so popular that some designs were created specifically for the export market. In places as far away as Europe, people began referring to the beautiful creations as "china."

Along with their artistic advancements, the Ming dynasty is also known for its extraordinary architecture. In addition to building the renowned Forbidden City, rulers from the Ming dynasty continued to extend and strengthen one of China's most widely known landmarks—the Great Wall. While construction of the wall had begun centuries earlier, the Ming emperors of the late 1400s repaired, rebuilt, and added on to the wall. The emperors were anxious to protect their territory, particularly from the Mongols in the north. The wall was greatly improved, and useful additions were made that also enhanced the wall's appearance. Shiny granite surfaces, tall watchtowers, and wide walkways turned the Great Wall into an impressive architectural wonder for all who saw it.

By 1644, trouble both at home and abroad plagued China and brought an end to the mighty Ming dynasty which had ruled over China for hundreds of years. Though this powerful dynasty may have ended, the impact of its leaders, traders, and artisans can still be seen today.

textContent.text: When I inherited my great-aunt's piano, I was thrilled and inspired. I remembered sitting in her living room, listening to her play wonderful melodies and watching her fingers fly across the keys. I was determined that I would finally learn to play the piano, too.

pieces.text: I tried teaching myself, using online instructional videos and different how-to books. I learned the basics, plunking out scales and some simple tunes. But I didn't feel like I was really making
. I felt discouraged. Maybe I just didn't have my great-aunt's musical touch.

textContent.text: Eventually, I called Melinda Canon, a piano teacher recommended to me by a friend. From my very first lesson with Melinda, I felt the joy of making music. We played simple yet magical duets together. She gave me useful pointers to refine my technique and suggested easy but inspiring classics for me to learn. With Melinda's expert guidance, I'm finally learning to make my great-aunt's piano sing again.

textContent.text: My friends and I love spending summer afternoons hanging out at Silver Seas Water Park. Last year, the water park was closed for renovations, so we were extra excited to go back this year. After scanning our season passes, we headed straight to our favorite water feature: the lazy river. Before we could recover from that shock, we were guided under a drenching waterfall—not relaxing at all! Apparently, the park has updated our beloved lazy river with some "refreshing" water features. Sadly, not all updates are improvements.

One, two, three, four, what do we need a pep squad for?

pieces.text: This question is nothing to cheer about, but it is the very question before our school board tonight. With cuts to the activities budget, the pep squad is first up on the chopping block.

textContent.text: Not everyone understands how important our pep squad is: we support our teams, we provide entertainment, and we build school spirit. Defunding the pep squad would devalue all that we do for this school.

Furthermore, members of our pep squad demonstrate the same dedication and discipline as athletes in any other sport. We work out three days a week, practice our routines daily, and compete in statewide competitions. More importantly, the leadership skills and character traits we develop—sportsmanship, enthusiasm, and self-confidence—will be valuable throughout our lives.

textContent.text: As a vegetarian, I've tried to incorporate tofu into my family's dinner plans. This protein-rich food has many health benefits. Furthermore, we've had delicious tofu dishes at restaurants, like Salsa Grill's amazing crispy tofu tacos. Yum!
Sadly, whenever I tried to make homemade tofu recipes, my tofu always came out soft, watery, and bland. That is, until I started using a tofu press!

My Veg-O tofu press works fabulously, but any similar device will suffice. To use the press, place a block of tofu between the plates and turn the screws to squeeze out excess moisture. Keep tightening the screws until your tofu is nice and firm, ready to soak up any delicious flavors you add to it.
Using a tofu press has opened up a whole new world of tofu-bilities—tofu stir-fries, tofu soups, and even tofu casseroles! Thanks to this simple, inexpensive gadget, tofu is back on the menu.

The Veg-O tofu press is the best device for making homemade stir-fries, soups, and casseroles.

textContent.text: Normally, I love the CinnaSandwich at Sunny's. I've long considered it the perfect breakfast treat. Sandwiched between the halves of a gooey cinnamon roll are two perfectly seasoned eggs and a generous mountain of crispy bacon, topped with melted cheese. For me, it's always been heaven on a plate.

In my past few visits to Sunny's, though, I've been sorely disappointed. My glorious sandwich has not been served in the delectable style I'm used to. First, it was served on a brioche bun instead of the delightful cinnamon roll, which is a key component of its deliciousness. On the next visit, the bacon was cold and limp. And last time, my cinnamon roll wasn't topped with its usual dollop of icing. Perhaps some additional training for new staff members could help return my beloved sandwich to its former glory.

textContent.text: Have you noticed anything amiss when driving down Oak Street recently? Where are the oaks? The city has been busily and methodically removing the big, beautiful trees that have lined the street for decades. Some of these trees are more than a century old, predating many businesses along this lovely cobblestone thoroughfare.

Why are these magnificent trees being felled? Are they diseased or dying? Do they present a danger to people along the street? No, the disturbing reason the city gives for the tree removal is money: Apparently, the annual pruning and mulching needed to maintain the trees is too expensive. It's cheaper to just chop them down.

This short-sighted decision to destroy these majestic giants is disastrous for the character of the city. These long-lived trees could and should grace Oak Street for generations to come. Please go to the "Save the Oaks" website to find out how you can join the effort to halt this tree-mendous tragedy.

The trees are beautiful, historic treasures, and the city should stop cutting them down.

textContent.text: I'm not often lured into candy stores, but the window of Brattle's Confectionery caught my eye. Inside, a man was cranking a wheel on a red machine to stretch a colorful rope of saltwater taffy. I just had to take a closer look.

I opened the door and walked right into an old-fashioned candy factory! The gleaming copper kettles looked original, probably from the mid-1900s. It was highly entertaining to watch the workers feed blocks of soft candy through antique brass rollers to be formed and cooled into lemon drops.

A woman in a clean white outfit offered me a delicious piece of dark chocolate and explained that Brattle's still makes everything the traditional way. I spent about an hour simply observing as the old machines churned out a variety of sweets. Candy stores are a dime a dozen, but Brattle's is truly one of a kind!

content.text: Which sentence best summarizes the author's point of view about Brattle's Confectionery?

choices.text: The old-fashioned store is fascinating, but their candy tastes the same as candy from a modern store.
The store is unique because the candies are made using old-fashioned equipment.

pieces.text: ? The answer isn't hard to find, even if it is in the dark. Just go outside at night, and look up. Very few places still have what you can see here: a dazzling display of stars and the Milky Way.

textContent.text: Our town has a rare opportunity to be named a Dark Sky Community by the International Dark-Sky Association. The process could take years; we'd have to adopt lighting restrictions and establish dark-sky educational programs.

It wouldn't be easy, but in return for our efforts, we'd get publicity that would bring tourists and businesses to Gull's Haven. People from light-drenched areas could come here for a dark respite under our beautiful night skies. Let's seize this chance to find a renewed purpose for Gull's Haven and preserve the wonder of our night sky for future generations.

textContent.text: I love skiing at Mount Prospect. The south side of the mountain has gentle slopes, which are labeled "green runs," for beginners and less adventurous skiers like me. You'll never find me on the mountain's north face with its steep "black diamond" slopes, which are for expert skiers.

Unfortunately, not all advanced skiers stay on the black diamond runs. I don't mind experienced skiers using the green runs for an occasional break, but they should show more courtesy. Recently, as I was enjoying my first-of-the-season glide down the "Easy Does It" run, I was suddenly cut off, without warning, by another skier racing past. Down I went in a jumble of twisted skis and knees. To make matters worse, a group of high-speed skiers whizzed past just as I was pulling myself up!
Please, expert skiers, when you ski on the green runs, slow down! You may be having some easy, fast fun, but you're ruining the slow-run fun for the rest of us.

content.text: Which sentence best summarizes the author's point of view about the expert skiers at Mount Prospect?

choices.text: They should slow down and be courteous to the less experienced skiers on the green ski runs.
They should be banned from the green ski runs, which should be reserved for beginners only.

textContent.text: My friends and I love spending summer afternoons hanging out at Silver Seas Water Park. Last year, the water park was closed for renovations, so we were extra excited to go back this year. After scanning our season passes, we headed straight to our favorite water feature: the lazy river. We've always enjoyed kicking back in our inner tubes, peacefully floating along the pool's winding path around the lush grounds.

The sparkling pool water looked so inviting! We hopped into our floats and settled in for a relaxing ride. How peaceful it was, slowly drifting along…until we rounded a bend and were suddenly blasted with ice-cold streams of water shooting from the sides of the pool. Before we could recover from that shock, we were guided under a drenching waterfall—not relaxing at all! Apparently, the park has updated our beloved lazy river with some "refreshing" water features. Sadly, not all updates are improvements.

choices.text: The lazy river feature is no longer as relaxing and enjoyable as it was in the past.
With its sparkling water and refreshing features, the lazy river is better than ever.

One, two, three, four, what do we need a pep squad for?

pieces.text: This question is nothing to cheer about, but it is the very question before our school board tonight. With cuts to the activities budget, the pep squad is first up on the chopping block.

textContent.text: Not everyone understands how important our pep squad is: we support our teams, we provide entertainment, and we build school spirit. Defunding the pep squad would devalue all that we do for this school.

Furthermore, members of our pep squad demonstrate the same dedication and discipline as athletes in any other sport. We work out three days a week, practice our routines daily, and compete in statewide competitions. More importantly, the leadership skills and character traits we develop—sportsmanship, enthusiasm, and self-confidence—will be valuable throughout our lives.

pieces.text: Instead of axing the pep squad entirely, why not cut a little from the budgets of all activities? It would be more reasonable for everyone to bear part of the budgetary pain. Together, we can make this work.

content.text: Which sentence best summarizes the author's point of view about cutting the pep squad from the school's activities budget?

choices.text: The pep squad should not have any cuts at all from its budget because it provides a great benefit to the school community.
Having a pep squad benefits the school and the members of the team, so it should not be completely cut from the budget.

textContent.text: As a vegetarian, I've tried to incorporate tofu into my family's dinner plans. This protein-rich food has many health benefits. Furthermore, we've had delicious tofu dishes at restaurants, like Salsa Grill's amazing crispy tofu tacos. Yum!
Sadly, whenever I tried to make homemade tofu recipes, my tofu always came out soft, watery, and bland. That is, until I started using a tofu press!

My Veg-O tofu press works fabulously, but any similar device will suffice. To use the press, place a block of tofu between the plates and turn the screws to squeeze out excess moisture. Keep tightening the screws until your tofu is nice and firm, ready to soak up any delicious flavors you add to it.
Using a tofu press has opened up a whole new world of tofu-bilities—tofu stir-fries, tofu soups, and even tofu casseroles! Thanks to this simple, inexpensive gadget, tofu is back on the menu.

content.text: Which sentence best summarizes the author's point of view about using a tofu press?

choices.text: A tofu press can help people make a variety of delicious tofu dishes similar to those in restaurants.
The Veg-O tofu press is the best device for making homemade stir-fries, soups, and casseroles.

textContent.text: Normally, I love the CinnaSandwich at Sunny's. I've long considered it the perfect breakfast treat. Sandwiched between the halves of a gooey cinnamon roll are two perfectly seasoned eggs and a generous mountain of crispy bacon, topped with melted cheese. For me, it's always been heaven on a plate.

In my past few visits to Sunny's, though, I've been sorely disappointed. My glorious sandwich has not been served in the delectable style I'm used to. First, it was served on a brioche bun instead of the delightful cinnamon roll, which is a key component of its deliciousness. On the next visit, the bacon was cold and limp. And last time, my cinnamon roll wasn't topped with its usual dollop of icing. Perhaps some additional training for new staff members could help return my beloved sandwich to its former glory.

textContent.text: My dog, Gigi, is so very gentle and sweet-natured that it's a little shocking what she does to her dog toys. No matter what the labels claim—like "the toughest toys for the toughest chewers"—she rips them to pieces within an hour, often within minutes.

I've searched everywhere for a longer-lasting dog toy, so I was excited to try the newest one from pet-goods company HardBitten. It's called "Tough Stuff," and as the name indicates, it's a stuffed toy, which Gigi loves best. It's even shaped like her favorite animal to menace: the squirrel.

pieces.text: Well, as advertised, this toy is virtually indestructible. After a week, it's still fully intact, nestled in Gigi's toy basket among the shredded remnants of her other toys. But alas, that's likely where it will stay. Gigi has completely lost interest in the toy; apparently, for her the best part of toys is tearing them to pieces. It seems the Tough Stuff toy is
tough, and what fun is that?

content.text: Which sentence best summarizes the author's point of view about the Tough Stuff dog toy?

choices.text: The toy is so difficult to destroy that it's not that much fun for some dogs to play with.
The toy is perfect for gentle, sweet-natured dogs who like to chew on something tough.

textContent.text: The campaign posters are all over school: Stay cool, vote for Jess Poole! Bank on Kat for Treasurer! Don't be shy, vote for Ty! It seems every candidate for class office is trying to outyell the others with bigger, flashier signs. As I navigate the hallways, it's like the walls are screaming at me.

pieces.text: Instead of trying to select class leaders based on these ridiculous posters, we need to know what the candidates believe—what they want to do for the class. It appears that many candidates just want to see their names plastered on the walls; they think the election is about
, not us.

textContent.text: The unfortunate thing is that this strategy works: name recognition gets people elected. But in an educational institution, we shouldn't validate this shallow thinking! Let's ditch campaign signs and meaningless slogans. Instead, let's put the candidates themselves on display in a series of debates and question-and-answer sessions. It's time to stop screaming and to start talking about the issues.

choices.text: School elections should focus on the issues and the voters, not on flashy campaigns.

textContent.text: I love skiing at Mount Prospect. The south side of the mountain has gentle slopes, which are labeled "green runs," for beginners and less adventurous skiers like me. You'll never find me on the mountain's north face with its steep "black diamond" slopes, which are for expert skiers.

Unfortunately, not all advanced skiers stay on the black diamond runs. I don't mind experienced skiers using the green runs for an occasional break, but they should show more courtesy. Recently, as I was enjoying my first-of-the-season glide down the "Easy Does It" run, I was suddenly cut off, without warning, by another skier racing past. Down I went in a jumble of twisted skis and knees. To make matters worse, a group of high-speed skiers whizzed past just as I was pulling myself up!
Please, expert skiers, when you ski on the green runs, slow down! You may be having some easy, fast fun, but you're ruining the slow-run fun for the rest of us.

textContent.text: I'm not often lured into candy stores, but the window of Brattle's Confectionery caught my eye. Inside, a man was cranking a wheel on a red machine to stretch a colorful rope of saltwater taffy. I just had to take a closer look.

I opened the door and walked right into an old-fashioned candy factory! The gleaming copper kettles looked original, probably from the mid-1900s. It was highly entertaining to watch the workers feed blocks of soft candy through antique brass rollers to be formed and cooled into lemon drops.

A woman in a clean white outfit offered me a delicious piece of dark chocolate and explained that Brattle's still makes everything the traditional way. I spent about an hour simply observing as the old machines churned out a variety of sweets. Candy stores are a dime a dozen, but Brattle's is truly one of a kind!

pieces.text: There's been a lot of talk lately about the future of our little town. Gull's Haven has certainly seen better times, and people often wonder,

content.text: What does our town have left to offer

pieces.text: ? The answer isn't hard to find, even if it is in the dark. Just go outside at night, and look up. Very few places still have what you can see here: a dazzling display of stars and the Milky Way.

textContent.text: Our town has a rare opportunity to be named a Dark Sky Community by the International Dark-Sky Association. The process could take years; we'd have to adopt lighting restrictions and establish dark-sky educational programs.

It wouldn't be easy, but in return for our efforts, we'd get publicity that would bring tourists and businesses to Gull's Haven. People from light-drenched areas could come here for a dark respite under our beautiful night skies. Let's seize this chance to find a renewed purpose for Gull's Haven and preserve the wonder of our night sky for future generations.

choices.text: The increase of tourists who want to gaze at the night sky would overwhelm the small town.
It would be worth the time and effort and would help revitalize the town.

textContent.text: Have you noticed anything amiss when driving down Oak Street recently? Where are the oaks? The city has been busily and methodically removing the big, beautiful trees that have lined the street for decades. Some of these trees are more than a century old, predating many businesses along this lovely cobblestone thoroughfare.

Why are these magnificent trees being felled? Are they diseased or dying? Do they present a danger to people along the street? No, the disturbing reason the city gives for the tree removal is money: Apparently, the annual pruning and mulching needed to maintain the trees is too expensive. It's cheaper to just chop them down.

This short-sighted decision to destroy these majestic giants is disastrous for the character of the city. These long-lived trees could and should grace Oak Street for generations to come. Please go to the "Save the Oaks" website to find out how you can join the effort to halt this tree-mendous tragedy.

textContent.text: My friends and I love spending summer afternoons hanging out at Silver Seas Water Park. Last year, the water park was closed for renovations, so we were extra excited to go back this year. After scanning our season passes, we headed straight to our favorite water feature: the lazy river. We've always enjoyed kicking back in our inner tubes, peacefully floating along the pool's winding path around the lush grounds.

The sparkling pool water looked so inviting! We hopped into our floats and settled in for a relaxing ride. How peaceful it was, slowly drifting along…until we rounded a bend and were suddenly blasted with ice-cold streams of water shooting from the sides of the pool. Before we could recover from that shock, we were guided under a drenching waterfall—not relaxing at all! Apparently, the park has updated our beloved lazy river with some "refreshing" water features. Sadly, not all updates are improvements.
